Lesson 3

Data Types and Encoding

Lesson introduction

Computers work with many kinds of data, such as numbers, words, and pictures. Inside the computer, all of this data is stored as 0s and 1s. This lesson explains data types, how data is shown in digital form, and how encoding turns letters into numbers.

Topics

  1. Data TypesThis part
  2. Digital Representation
  3. Encoding

Objectives and outcomes

Lesson objectives

  • Explain what a data type is.
  • Describe how computers store data using 0s and 1s.
  • Identify simple encoding systems such as ASCII and Unicode.

Lesson outcomes

  • Students can name common data types.
  • Students can explain why computers use binary.
  • Students can describe how letters are turned into numbers.

Topic 1

1. Data Types

A data type tells the computer what kind of data it is storing. Each data type is stored and used in its own way. Choosing the right data type helps programs work correctly.

1.1 Common Data Types

An integer stores whole numbers, like 7 or 120. A real (or float) number has a decimal point, like 3.5. A character stores one letter or symbol, a string stores text like "Hello", and a Boolean stores only True or False.

Data typeStoresExample
IntegerWhole numbers7, 120
Real (float)Numbers with a decimal point3.5
CharacterOne letter or symbolA
StringText"Hello"
BooleanOnly True or FalseTrue, False

1.2 Why Data Types Matter

Data types tell the computer how much memory to use and what it can do with the data. For example, two numbers can be added together, but two words cannot. Using the wrong data type can cause errors.

Algorithm

Lab-1: Working Process of Storing Data

Goal

See the easy steps a computer follows to store a piece of data.

Steps

  1. The user types data into a program.
  2. The program checks what kind of data it is.
  3. The program chooses the matching data type.
  4. The computer gives the data space in memory.
  5. The data is changed into binary.
  6. The binary is saved in memory.
  7. The program can now use the data.
  8. The data stays saved until it is changed or deleted.

Final process

Data→Data Type→Binary→Memory

Summary

Heading and one-line definition

Heading / SubheadingOne-Line Definition
1. Data TypesA data type tells the computer what kind of data it is storing.
1.1 Common Data TypesInteger, real, character, string, and Boolean are common data types.
1.2 Why Data Types MatterData types decide how data is stored and what can be done with it.
Lab-1: Storing DataShows the easy steps a computer follows to store data.

Lesson 3

Data Types and Encoding

Lesson introduction

Computers work with many kinds of data, such as numbers, words, and pictures. Inside the computer, all of this data is stored as 0s and 1s. This lesson explains data types, how data is shown in digital form, and how encoding turns letters into numbers.

Topics

  1. Data Types
  2. Digital RepresentationThis part
  3. Encoding

Objectives and outcomes

Lesson objectives

  • Explain what a data type is.
  • Describe how computers store data using 0s and 1s.
  • Identify simple encoding systems such as ASCII and Unicode.

Lesson outcomes

  • Students can name common data types.
  • Students can explain why computers use binary.
  • Students can describe how letters are turned into numbers.

Topic 2

2. Digital Representation

Computers are digital machines. They store all data using only two digits, 0 and 1. This number system is called binary.

2.1 Bits and Bytes

A bit is the smallest unit of data, and it can be 0 or 1. A group of 8 bits is called a byte, and one byte can store one letter. Bigger units include kilobytes (KB), megabytes (MB), and gigabytes (GB).

UnitMeaning
BitThe smallest unit: 0 or 1
Byte8 bits, enough for one letter
KB, MB, GBKilobytes, megabytes, gigabytes

2.2 Binary Numbers

Binary is a base-2 system. Each place value is double the one before it: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and so on. For example, the decimal number 5 is written as 101 in binary (4 + 0 + 1).

Place values for 5 = 101

160
80
41
20
11

Algorithm

Lab-2: Working Process of Converting a Number to Binary

Goal

See the easy steps to change a decimal number into binary.

Steps

  1. Start with a decimal number, like 13.
  2. Divide the number by 2.
  3. Write down the remainder (0 or 1).
  4. Use the answer as the new number.
  5. Repeat until the number becomes 0.
  6. Read the remainders from bottom to top.
  7. The result is the binary number.
  8. Example: 13 becomes 1101 in binary.

Final process

Decimal→Divide by 2→Remainders→Binary

Summary

Heading and one-line definition

Heading / SubheadingOne-Line Definition
2. Digital RepresentationComputers store all data using only 0s and 1s, called binary.
2.1 Bits and BytesA bit is a single 0 or 1, and a byte is a group of 8 bits.
2.2 Binary NumbersBinary is a base-2 system where each place value doubles.
Lab-2: Number to BinaryShows the easy steps to change a decimal number into binary.

Lesson 3

Data Types and Encoding

Lesson introduction

Computers work with many kinds of data, such as numbers, words, and pictures. Inside the computer, all of this data is stored as 0s and 1s. This lesson explains data types, how data is shown in digital form, and how encoding turns letters into numbers.

Topics

  1. Data Types
  2. Digital Representation
  3. EncodingThis part

Objectives and outcomes

Lesson objectives

  • Explain what a data type is.
  • Describe how computers store data using 0s and 1s.
  • Identify simple encoding systems such as ASCII and Unicode.

Lesson outcomes

  • Students can name common data types.
  • Students can explain why computers use binary.
  • Students can describe how letters are turned into numbers.

Topic 3

3. Encoding

Encoding means changing data into a code that the computer can store. Each letter, digit, or symbol is given its own number. That number is then stored in binary.

Letter→Number→Binary

3.1 ASCII

ASCII is a simple code for English letters, digits, and symbols. It has 128 characters. For example, the capital letter A has the code 65, which is 01000001 in binary.

A→65→01000001

3.2 Unicode

Unicode is a much bigger code. It covers letters from almost every language, including Arabic, and even emojis. This lets people share text in any language on any computer.

Algorithm

Lab-3: Working Process of Encoding a Letter

Goal

See the easy steps a computer follows when a letter is typed.

Steps

  1. The user presses a key, like A.
  2. The keyboard sends a signal to the computer.
  3. The Operating System finds the character code for A.
  4. In ASCII, the code for A is 65.
  5. The number 65 is changed into binary: 01000001.
  6. The binary is saved in memory.
  7. The letter is ready to be shown or saved.
  8. The same code is used every time A is typed.

Final process

Key→Character Code→Binary→Memory

Algorithm

Lab-4: Working Process of Showing Text on the Screen

Goal

See the easy steps a computer follows to turn binary back into text.

Steps

  1. The program reads binary data from memory.
  2. The computer groups the bits into bytes.
  3. Each byte is matched to a character code.
  4. The encoding table (ASCII or Unicode) finds the matching letter.
  5. The computer chooses the letter shape from a font.
  6. The letter appears on the screen.
  7. The user can now read the text.
  8. If the wrong encoding is used, strange symbols may appear.

Final process

Binary→Character Code→Letter→Screen

Side by side

Lab-3 and Lab-4 compared

#Lab-3: Encoding a letterLab-4: Showing text
1The user presses a key, like A.The program reads binary data from memory.
2The keyboard sends a signal to the computer.The computer groups the bits into bytes.
3The Operating System finds the character code for A.Each byte is matched to a character code.
4In ASCII, the code for A is 65.The encoding table (ASCII or Unicode) finds the matching letter.
5The number 65 is changed into binary: 01000001.The computer chooses the letter shape from a font.
6The binary is saved in memory.The letter appears on the screen.
7The letter is ready to be shown or saved.The user can now read the text.
8The same code is used every time A is typed.If the wrong encoding is used, strange symbols may appear.

Summary

Heading and one-line definition

Heading / SubheadingOne-Line Definition
3. EncodingEncoding gives each letter or symbol a number stored in binary.
3.1 ASCIIASCII is a simple 128-character code for English text.
3.2 UnicodeUnicode is a large code that covers almost every language.
Lab-3: Encoding a LetterShows the easy steps a computer follows when a letter is typed.
Lab-4: Showing TextShows the easy steps a computer follows to show text on the screen.

chips.text: The program reads binary data from memory.
The computer groups the bits into bytes.
Each byte is matched to a character code.
The encoding table (ASCII or Unicode) finds the matching letter.
The computer chooses the letter shape from a font.
The letter appears on the screen.
The user can now read the text.
If the wrong encoding is used, strange symbols may appear.
